strengths: First real-world aerial 3D semantic scene completion benchmark, addressing a clear gap in the literature for UAV/drone-based 3D perception research
Practical image-based data generation framework that minimizes manual annotation by leveraging 2D-to-3D projection, avoiding expensive LiDAR hardware requirements
Comprehensive scale and diversity: 20,000+ samples across multiple altitudes (30m, 40m, 50m), seasons, and diverse environments (urban, industrial, rural) with high-resolution input imagery
High geometric fidelity demonstrated by 1.24 pixel average reprojection error and strong 3D reconstruction quality with >90% image overlap across scenes
Well-designed multi-dimensional evaluation framework including class-wise, group-wise, and altitude-wise analysis, supplemented by metric depth estimation benchmarking
Excellent reproducibility: detailed implementation documentation, supplementary material with semantic class distributions and per-scene statistics, and promised code/data release
Addresses practical needs for autonomous systems and robotics requiring holistic 3D scene understanding from aerial perspectives without LiDAR
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty—data generation pipeline relies entirely on established techniques (SfM, Poisson reconstruction, silhouette carving) with minimal novel algorithmic contributions specific to aerial 3D understanding

Insufficient baseline evaluation: only CCGFormer is benchmarked without comparisons to other recent SSC methods, ablations on pipeline design choices, or evidence the dataset reveals unique aerial-specific challenges

Ground-truth quality not independently validated—multi-stage pipeline (SfM→reconstruction→annotation→voxelization) introduces potential error accumulation; reprojection error alone does not ensure semantic accuracy; inter-annotator agreement and annotation guidelines not documented
Severe class imbalance (Building 75.7%, Flying Animal 0.001%) inadequately addressed with no documented strategies for balanced training/evaluation or analysis of impact on rare-class performance
Geographic scope extremely limited to 9 scenes in a single region, raising critical generalization concerns—unclear whether models will transfer to different regions, climates, or urban layouts

Overstated annotation efficiency: requires manual 2D semantic segmentation for ~10% of images per scene; the 2D-to-3D lifting depends on reconstruction quality and becomes a bottleneck for dataset extension

Depth estimation results (Table 4) show significant altitude-dependent performance degradation and dramatic improvement with in-domain fine-tuning, suggesting potential metric inconsistencies or domain gaps that are not thoroughly explained

Limited analysis of aerial-specific challenges and failure modes: no systematic study of how aerial perspective differs from ground-based SSC (different occlusion patterns, atmospheric effects, scale variations), no error analysis, and no justification of design choices (scene selection, altitude values, class taxonomy)
Missing ablations on data generation pipeline (voxel size, reconstruction parameters, densification strategies) and no analysis of how design choices impact final semantic quality
Minimal discussion articulating what specific research gaps OccuFly uniquely addresses beyond being the 'first aerial SSC dataset'

strengths: Addresses important gap: first real-world aerial 3D semantic scene completion benchmark, relevant for autonomous aerial systems and surveillance applications

Large-scale, well-constructed dataset: 20,000+ samples spanning ~200,000 m², 22 semantic classes, multiple altitudes, and seasonal variations with demonstrated geometric fidelity (1.24 pixel reprojection error)
Practical camera-based data generation: clever framework avoiding expensive LiDAR hardware by lifting 2D annotations to 3D with ~99% automatic label coverage
Comprehensive benchmark evaluation: thorough analysis with per-class, per-altitude, and per-group metrics (Fig. 3), plus cross-domain evaluation with metric depth estimation
Commitment to reproducibility and community contribution through promised code and dataset release
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: paper is primarily a dataset contribution using standard techniques (SfM, Poisson reconstruction, DBSCAN) in straightforward combinations with no novel methods proposed to address aerial-specific SSC challenges

Severe and unaddressed class imbalance: Building dominates at 75.75% while Bicycle (0.0048%) and Person (0.0002%) are underrepresented, making evaluation unreliable for minority classes without mitigation strategies discussed

Methodological concerns with 2D-to-3D label lifting: using 2D segmentation as intermediate introduces systematic biases not validated; no analysis of label transfer errors, boundary artifacts, or whether 2D method quality assumptions hold for 3D
Limited scene diversity: only 9 scenes despite 20,000+ samples from single geographic region with unclear seasonal distribution, limiting generalization claims

Shallow analysis of benchmark results: paper shows existing methods fail on aerial data but doesn't explain why, investigate failure modes, or propose solutions for aerial-specific challenges (viewpoint, occlusion patterns, scale variations)

Insufficient scope of baseline evaluation: only 2 methods thoroughly evaluated (CCGFormer, DAV2); missing comparisons with recent SSC approaches and lacking analysis of domain shift from terrestrial to aerial

Scalability limitations: semi-manual annotation process (~10% of images per scene) doesn't scale to new regions; requires expensive hardware (DJI UAVs, GNSS units) limiting reproducibility compared to simpler approaches

Missing critical technical analyses: no computational cost evaluation, limited investigation of altitude-dependent performance variations (Table 4 shows large error ranges), no error distribution analysis beyond class-wise metrics, insufficient failure case discussion

strengths: First real-world aerial 3D Semantic Scene Completion benchmark—addresses a clear gap in the literature for aerial perspective 3D understanding
Large-scale, diverse dataset: 20,000+ samples covering ~200,000m² across three altitudes, four seasons, and three environment types (urban, industrial, rural)
Practical and scalable data generation framework using image-based SfM reconstruction with efficient label lifting (<10% manual annotation, >99% automatic labeling), avoiding costly LiDAR hardware
Comprehensive multi-dimensional evaluation: class-wise, group-wise, and altitude-wise metrics revealing important biases and correlations natural to aerial data
Strong statistical documentation and high-quality visualizations (Figures 4-10, Tables 1-11) demonstrating data quality, reconstruction fidelity, and per-scene metrics
Good reproducibility: detailed implementation sections, promised code/dataset release, clear experimental setup and hyperparameters
Addresses practical applications in autonomous aerial systems, UAV-based surveillance, and urban planning—timely and impactful contribution
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: data generation relies on standard techniques (SfM, kNN label transfer, DBSCAN). Primarily benchmarks existing methods rather than proposing new approaches

Insufficient analysis of data generation quality: no inter-annotator agreement, no ablation studies on kNN parameter choices (k=100, k=200), missing sensitivity analysis on DBSCAN parameters (ε, MinPts)

Reconstruction quality concerns inadequately addressed: Figure 7 shows depth distributions but lacks per-altitude and per-class SfM reconstruction error analysis. How do errors propagate to semantic labels?

Limited baseline evaluation: only two main methods benchmarked (CCGFormer for SSC, DAv2 for depth). No cross-domain evaluation (terrestrial SSC models on aerial data) or comparison with other aerial 3D methods

Significant class imbalance not adequately discussed: Figure 3 shows extreme imbalance (flying animals, persons <0.01%). Strong correlation between class frequency and performance suggests potential benchmark artifacts. No class rebalancing strategies discussed
Potential dataset biases: single geographic region, unclear seasonal distribution, no analysis of geographic or environmental generalization
Voxelization choice (25cm edge length) and metric depth map generation (Sec. 3.3.4) lack justification and validation

Important technical details relegated to supplementary material: better integration of reconstruction error analysis and per-altitude performance breakdown into main paper would strengthen technical depth

strengths: First real-world aerial SSC benchmark addressing a significant gap for autonomous aerial vehicles, with no direct competitors in the aerial domain
Large-scale, well-curated dataset: 20,000+ samples across 9 diverse scenes with multi-seasonal coverage and three environmental types (urban, industrial, rural)
Practical image-based data generation framework that leverages photogrammetry to automate ground-truth creation with <10% manual annotation, avoiding LiDAR sparsity limitations
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: benchmark suite covers multiple methods, altitude-wise metrics, class-wise analysis, and qualitative assessments revealing domain-specific challenges
High geometric fidelity demonstrated by 92% pixel-wise agreement in 3D reconstruction and 1.24-pixel average reprojection error
Thorough technical soundness: well-formulated problem statement, careful class-aware voxelization methodology, proper handling of surface/occluded/invalid voxel classes
Excellent reproducibility: detailed implementation specifications, dataset statistics, clear procedural documentation, and extensive visualization of data quality across 21 semantic classes
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: relies on commercial SfM software (Metashape), uses standard majority voting for label transfer, and employs conventional voxelization procedures without algorithmic innovation
Manual annotation overhead remains significant (9.17% on average at ~29 minutes per image), limiting scalability to larger geographic regions and creating bottleneck in data expansion
Narrow geographic scope: all 9 scenes from single region (Ingolstadt, Germany); limited altitude range (predominantly 30-50m, max ~80m); lack of geographic diversity limits generalization claims
Circular evaluation dependency: metric depth maps are derived from the same photogrammetric reconstruction that serves as ground-truth, potentially inflating reported quality metrics

Incomplete analysis of key findings: altitude-induced performance degradation documented but not mechanistically analyzed; severe underperformance of modern methods (DepthAnything v2) lacks investigation

Missing ablation studies on data generation pipeline components; no systematic analysis of reconstruction failures in textureless or repetitive regions; reconstruction error propagation to downstream tasks not characterized

Evaluated methods are primarily terrestrial SSC models without aerial adaptation; no baseline methods specifically designed for aerial domain; limited insights into required architectural modifications for aerial transfer

Data generation framework dependencies not fully transparent: requires >90% image overlap (operationally impractical), relies on commercial software, and kNN refinement parameters (k=100, ε=20) lack justification

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap by introducing the first real-world aerial 3D SSC benchmark dataset, filling an important need for aerial vision research
Well-designed data acquisition protocol with multiple altitudes, seasons, diverse environments, and proper RTK-GPS geodetic referencing
Clever camera-based data generation framework avoiding LiDAR sparsity issues through multi-view SfM and semantic label transfer
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with systematic benchmarking of multiple methods and altitude/class-wise performance analysis
Large-scale dataset with 20,000+ samples, 21 semantic classes, and metric depth maps for aerial scenes
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: entire framework relies on established techniques (classical SfM, Poisson reconstruction, k-NN voting) with no novel methodology or algorithmic contribution
Severe manual annotation burden underdisclosed: despite '< 10% manual annotation' claims, actual effort is ~29 min/image (~1.3 days/scene), substantially contradicting efficiency claims
Critical ground truth quality issues: metric depth maps have 25-50% scale deviations and systematic errors increasing with altitude, undermining benchmark reliability
Poor baseline performance is concerning: existing methods achieve only 10-20% mIoU and 26-35% depth RMSE even after fine-tuning, raising questions about dataset usability and annotation quality
Severe class imbalance with 11 classes at <0.1% frequency while Building/Grass/Roof dominate (>62%), making balanced evaluation impossible
Limited dataset scale: only 9 unique scenes despite 20,000+ samples makes generalization difficult and vulnerable to overfitting in modern deep learning contexts
Missing critical analysis: no systematic failure case analysis, limited explanation of why methods fail so dramatically on aerial data, and no clear pathforward for future work
Incomplete practical validation: no downstream task evaluation or demonstration that models trained on OccuFly generalize better than terrestrial SSC training
Reproducibility concerns: data/code availability not mentioned, RTK precision incomplete, manual annotation selection strategy unclear, and implementation details limited
Presentation issues: Figure 2 is overly complex, methodology section uses heavy notation, and paper tries to cover too much ground reducing focus and clarity

strengths: Addresses a critical gap: First real-world aerial 3D Semantic Scene Completion benchmark, filling an important niche for autonomous aerial systems and UAV research
Practical LiDAR-free data generation framework that reduces hardware constraints for UAV platforms, addressing real limitations of aerial systems
Large-scale real-world dataset: 20,000+ samples across 9 scenes with multiple altitudes, seasons, and 21 semantic classes providing diverse evaluation conditions
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: Multiple methods tested with altitude-wise and class-wise analysis, revealing systematic challenges in aerial perception
Honest and transparent reporting: Authors explicitly discuss fundamental limitations (metric depth estimation failures, altitude-dependent degradation) rather than overstating results
Technical soundness: Well-motivated methodology with clear problem formulation, proper ground truth generation with visibility/occlusion handling, and detailed implementation transparency
High-quality presentation: Exceptional visualizations (especially Figure 6), clear mathematical notation, well-organized structure, and extensive supplementary materials
weaknesses: Limited geographic and climatic diversity: All 9 scenes from a single city (Ingolstadt, Germany) with no cross-region evaluation, severely limiting generalization claims
Severe annotation scalability bottleneck: <10% manual annotation ratio requiring ~29 minutes per image with only 9.17% efficiency (Table 9), making dataset expansion impractical
Modest dataset scale: 20,000 samples is substantially smaller than modern vision benchmarks (typically 1M+), potentially constraining deep learning model training
Inadequate depth estimation solutions: Paper acknowledges severe limitations in metric monocular depth in aerial settings but proposes no remedies or alternative approaches
Weak quantitative results: Best performance ~52% mIoU at 50m altitude indicates large unsolved challenges, raising questions about dataset utility for practical applications
Limited technical novelty: Beyond the dataset, contributions are incremental (standard MVS reconstruction, straightforward kNN semantic propagation with no algorithmic innovations)
Missing robustness and generalization analysis: No cross-dataset evaluation, synthetic-to-real transfer studies, or systematic failure mode analysis beyond altitude trends
Unanalyzed kNN propagation errors: Semantic label transfer methodology could introduce systematic biases, but error propagation through the pipeline is not quantified
Reproducibility concerns: Dataset release status unclear, some implementation details (exact MVS parameters, kNN definitions) could be more explicit, no mentioned licensing constraints
